v: Forget the impossible hype and watch what is actually there: a slow, emotional family drama inside a mafia backdrop, with Rajini finally getting room to ACT and Radhika Apte at times dominating even him.
e: Kabali is not the nonstop Rajini-style mass film the gigantic pre-release expectations conditioned many viewers to expect. Going in with zero expectations, I found a good, deliberately slow family story inside a gangster setting, with Rajinikanth showing vulnerability and acting rather than relying only on trademark style, and Radhika Apte giving him formidable company.
body:
Maybe it was time for the Superstar to take a small break and let his confused audience decide exactly what kind of roles they wanted their ageing icon to play 😄

Thanks to all the negative buzz, I entered Kabali with zero expectations.

What I saw on screen was actually a beautiful family drama with emotions, placed against a mafia backdrop.

Yes, the movie is sloooooow.

But that kind of deliberate pace is hardly unusual in Tamil cinema.

More importantly, Rajini nails the acting — not through his regular style tricks, but by getting the rare opportunity to show vulnerability.

I genuinely had to think back and ask myself when we had last seen a Rajinikanth film give him this much space to perform, especially in scenes such as Kabali’s desperate search for his wife.

Special mention to Radhika Apte.

She is so strong that at times she completely dominates Rajini in sheer screen presence.

I also heard people blaming the PR team for creating unreasonable expectations around the movie.

Come on — how much conventional promotion was actually done?

The team released a teaser, not even a full trailer; there was no giant audio launch and Rajini was not sitting through endless promotional interviews.

The truth is that everyone around us wanted a little limelight simply by attaching themselves to the name RAJINI, and the hype became self-generating.

So relax and enjoy the acting treat of Rajini daaa.

The first and final fifteen minutes give hardcore mass fans some of the Superstar flavour they came for.

In between, there is a good family story narrated slowly and supported by superb performances from Rajini and Radhika.

v: Simply SUPERB!!! Nani’s acting is a full meal, Mani Sharma’s BGM is terrific and I did not have a single boring moment. Hero aa? Villain aa? Forget both — NANI oka goppa ACTOR!!!!!
e: Gentleman felt wonderfully refreshing after a stretch of exhausting mainstream films. The different concept kept me engaged without a single boring stretch, Mani Sharma’s background score works beautifully and the supporting cast adds value — but the complete meal is Nani, once again proving that the hero-versus-villain label matters far less than the actor inside both possibilities.
body:
Simply SUPERB!!!!!

Nani’s acting is FULL MEALS.

Mani Sharma’s BGM is superb too.

Special mention also goes to Srinivas Avasarala and the heroine, who both add nicely to the experience.

Personally, I did not have a single boring moment in the entire movie.

After sitting through kalaa khandalu like Sardaar Gabbar Singh, Brahmotsavam and Sarrainodu 😄, a film with a genuinely different concept felt especially refreshing.

But ultimately, Gentleman comes back to one man.

NANI hero no… villain no… kaadhu.

Oka GOPPA ACTOR!!!!!

v: I apologised for commenting before watching because seeing the movie revealed the true horror 😄 No story, endless relatives, recycled Mahesh emotions and family-value lectures stretched so far that even TV serial editors might cut two hours out.
e: Brahmotsavam triggered one of my longest rants because I could find almost nothing to defend beyond the Bala Tripuramani song and Mahesh Babu trying something slightly different there. The screenplay feels shapeless, the huge cast and lavish settings add expense rather than value, familiar emotional beats repeat without impact and the film mistakes family-value speeches for actual storytelling.
body:
CAUTION: I do not think I wrote paragraphs this long even in my B.Tech answer sheets, so read this at your own risk 😄

Before watching Brahmotsavam, a few fans told me I had no right to comment without seeing the film.

At first I thought they were merely being defensive.

After watching it, I understood their point completely.

How can you describe narakam properly without first seeing it up close? 😄

So I sincerely apologise for my earlier comments creating even the faint impression that the movie might be okay.

Now to the actual review.

Just because films like SVSC and Srimanthudu worked does not mean you can put Mahesh Babu at the centre, surround him with a lorry-load of relatives, give him the same smile and congested emotional voice, and expect audiences to keep accepting it.

I watch a Mahesh film because I know what kind of performances he has delivered in movies such as Nijam, Okkadu, Pokiri, Businessman and 1: Nenokkadine.

Here, apart from the familiar crying-tone scenes around the interval and climax, I found very little that really used the actor.

If the only argument is that Babu looks handsome, then buying a Mahesh poster and putting it in the bedroom is much cheaper than making an entire movie around that fact 😄

There are also scenes whose emotional logic simply baffled me.

When the father suddenly collapses, instead of behaving like somebody in a medical emergency the hero almost appears to ask him for one final good family-values speech.

Then comes the usual debate about responsibility.

If a film becomes a hit, everybody praises the hero’s brilliant script-selection skills.

If it becomes a disaster, suddenly only the director is responsible?

Distributors invest in a major Mahesh film because Mahesh is attached to it, so the star also has a responsibility to choose carefully.

The one thing I genuinely liked is the Bala Tripuramani song.

At least there, Mahesh tries something noticeably different.

Some people also claimed that only audiences who do not understand family values were spreading negativity about the film.

Fair enough — after watching Brahmotsavam, my brother and I, normally busy with our own lives, actually called each other to ask, “Rey, cinema chusava? Baane unnava?” 😛

So perhaps it did improve family communication after all.

Coming to the production: having money is wonderful, but spending it intelligently is even better.

Huge crowds, giant settings and more than a hundred shooting days do not automatically create a memorable family epic.

At some point somebody should have asked whether all those actors and all that scale were actually helping the story.

And Srikanth Addala — after Kotha Bangaru Lokam, I kept waiting for the writing to become tighter rather than increasingly dependent on dialect-heavy philosophical conversations without enough plot underneath them.

People outside were calling Brahmotsavam a television serial.

Please do not insult serials like that.

Even a serial editor might remove two hours from this material and use the remaining thirty minutes as an episode 😄

If you are going to make something this routine, even a straightforward mass entertainer may at least give B and C centres a reason to keep watching.

Trying to depend entirely on a so-called class audience without giving them a coherent film is much riskier.

For me, this was an exhausting lesson in how scale, stars, relatives and good intentions cannot substitute for an actual screenplay.

v: SHELL SHOCKED!!!!! How do you write something this complex and explain it as easily as peeling a banana for a child? Take a BOW, Vikram Kumar and team — and huge respect to Suriya for betting his own money and stardom on this kind of idea.
e: 24 stunned me because Vikram Kumar takes a complicated time-travel story and communicates it with remarkable clarity. Suriya deserves enormous credit not only for performing it but for backing such an ambitious concept as producer. The CG could be better and the romance trimmed, but those reservations barely matter beside the excitement of seeing mainstream South Indian cinema attempt something this fresh.
body:
SHELL SHOCKED!!!!!

How does somebody write a story this COMPLEX… and then explain it to an audience so simply?

It almost feels like peeling a banana and handing it to a small child 😄

Take a BOW, Vikram Kumar and team!!!!!

And Suriya — it takes real GUTS to accept a story like this without first worrying about all the logistical complications.

It takes even more conviction to put your own hard-earned money behind that ambition as a producer rather than merely calling yourself one because you sacrificed part of a star salary.

The CG could definitely have been better.

The romance track could also have been trimmed.

But honestly… who cares!!!!!

For Telugu-film audiences at that point, ideas and execution like this still felt wonderfully new.

That freshness, and the clarity with which such a complicated concept reaches the audience, overwhelmed the relatively small imperfections for me.
